lessons.title: Reading rwx, octal modes and directory permissions
lessons.goal:
Learn to read `ls -l`, to change permissions with `chmod` in both symbolic and octal form, and to know what `r`, `w` and `x` mean on a directory.

Why it matters: "Permission denied" is one of the most common errors. You can fix it correctly only if you can read the mode.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. Some steps use sudo; run those on a machine where that is safe.

steps.title: Ten characters
steps.text: `ls -l` starts with the file type (`-` file, `d` directory) and nine permission characters: **owner**, **group**, **others**. Each triple is `r` (read), `w` (write), `x` (execute).

run.output:
drwxr-xr-x. 2 opc opc 6 Nov  8 10:36 d
-rw-r--r--. 1 opc opc 0 Nov  8 10:36 f.txt

steps.title: Octal: r=4, w=2, x=1
steps.text: Add the numbers per triple. `rw-` = 4+2 = 6, `r--` = 4, `---` = 0. So `rw-r-----` is `640`. `stat -c %a` prints the octal form.

steps.title: Symbolic form changes only what you name
steps.text: `u` owner, `g` group, `o` others, `a` all. `+` adds, `-` removes, `=` sets. Use it when you want to change one bit and keep the rest.

steps.title: What the bits mean on a directory
steps.text: On a directory: `r` = list the names, `x` = enter it and reach files inside by name, `w` = create, delete and rename entries (needs `x` too).

run.cmd: chmod u-x d; ls d; cat d/file.txt
chmod u+x,u-r d; ls d; cat d/file.txt
run.output:
ls: cannot open directory 'd': Permission denied
secret

steps.after: Without `x` you can do nothing inside. Without `r` but with `x` you can open a file if you know its name, but you cannot list the directory.

steps.title: umask removes bits from new files
steps.text: New files start at `666` and new directories at `777`. The **umask** is subtracted. With `022` you get `644` and `755`.

run.cmd: touch new.txt; mkdir newdir; stat -c '%a %n' new.txt newdir

steps.under: `open()` and `mkdir()` take a requested mode. The kernel applies `mode & ~umask`. The umask is a property of the process and is inherited by children, so `(umask 077; ...)` in a subshell does not change your shell.

quiz.q: What is the octal mode of `rwxr-x---`?
A directory has `r--` for you but no `x`. What can you do?
options: List names but not read the files' metadata or open files
quiz.explain: `r` lists names. Without `x` you cannot access anything inside by path. In the lesson `ls d` could still list the name, but `cat d/file.txt` failed with Permission denied.

quiz.q: The umask is 027. What mode does a new file get?
Which command adds execute for the owner and changes nothing else?

check.scenario: A web server returns 403 for /srv/www/site/index.html. The file is 644 and owned by you. What else must you check?
check.answer: Every **directory** on the path needs `x` for the server's user: `/srv`, `/srv/www`, `/srv/www/site`. Check with `namei -l /srv/www/site/index.html`, which shows the mode of each component.

lessons.title: Who is checked: owner, group, other, and ownership
lessons.goal:
Learn how the kernel picks which permission triple applies, and how ownership changes.

Why it matters: the rule has a surprise (the owner can be locked out while the group can read), and knowing it saves hours of debugging.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. Some steps use sudo; run those on a machine where that is safe.

steps.title: Your identity
steps.text: Every process has a user ID (UID) and group IDs (GIDs). `id` shows them. Files store a numeric owner and group.

steps.title: The kernel checks one class only
steps.text: The kernel tests in order: are you the **owner**? Then only the owner bits apply. Else are you in the **group**? Then only the group bits. Else the **other** bits. It stops at the first match.
steps.after: You own the file and belong to its group, and the group has full rights, but you are denied. The owner triple `---` matched first.

steps.title: chown and chgrp change ownership
steps.text: Only root can give a file to another user. The owner can change the group to any group they belong to.

run.cmd: sudo chown root:adm rule.txt; ls -l rule.txt
sudo chown opc:opc rule.txt; ls -l rule.txt

steps.title: Test as another user
steps.text: `sudo -u USER` runs a command as that user, which is the best way to test permissions.

run.cmd: chmod 644 rule.txt; sudo -u nobody cat rule.txt

steps.under: Permission checks happen inside the kernel on every `open()`. The kernel compares the process's **filesystem UID/GID and supplementary groups** with the inode's owner, group and mode bits. Root skips the read/write checks through the `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` capability (module 34).

quiz.q: A file is `---rwxrwx` and you are its owner. Can you read it?
options: Yes, you are in the group
quiz.explain: The kernel stops at the owner class.

quiz.q: Who may change a file's owner to another user?
Which command lets you test file access as the user `nobody`?

check.scenario: Everything in a shared project directory should be editable by the group `dev`, but new files come out as 644 and owned by their creator's group. Which two settings fix this?
check.answer:
1. The **setgid bit** on the directory (`chmod g+s dir`) so new files inherit the directory's group.
2. A **umask of 002** for the users (or a default ACL, next lesson) so new files are group-writable.

lessons.title: setuid, setgid, sticky, ACLs and file attributes
lessons.goal:
Learn the three special mode bits, extended ACLs and the immutable attribute, and see each one working.

Why it matters: these are how `passwd` can edit `/etc/shadow`, how `/tmp` stays safe, and how a file can be undeletable even by root. Misused setuid files are a classic privilege-escalation path.

setup.note: Use a scratch directory. Some steps use sudo; run those on a machine where that is safe.

steps.title: setuid runs a program as its owner
steps.text: A program with the **setuid** bit runs with the file owner's identity, not yours. `passwd` is owned by root and has `s` in the owner triple, so it can write `/etc/shadow`.

steps.title: A demo program: real and effective UID
steps.text: This program prints the real UID (who started it) and the effective UID (whose rights it has). Save as `ids.c` and compile it.

steps.title: Turn on setuid and run it again
steps.text: We make root the owner and set the bit. The effective UID becomes 0 while the real UID stays yours.

run.cmd: sudo chown root:root ids && sudo chmod u+s ids

steps.under: At `execve`, if the file has the setuid bit, the kernel sets the process's effective UID (and saved UID) to the file's owner. The real UID is unchanged. Nosuid mounts and scripts (the kernel ignores setuid on scripts) are limits.

steps.title: setgid on a directory, and the sticky bit
steps.text: On a directory, **setgid** makes new files inherit the directory's group (`adm` here, instead of your own group `opc`). **sticky** (`t`) lets only owners delete their entries.

run.cmd: mkdir share && chgrp adm share && chmod 2775 share && ls -ld share

run.output:
opc opc plain.txt
opc adm share/x

steps.title: ACLs add per-user rules
steps.text: A POSIX **ACL** gives rights to extra users or groups without changing the owner or group. `setfacl -m` modifies, `getfacl` shows. `ls -l` marks a file with ACL by a `+`.

run.cmd: echo hi > acl.txt; chmod 600 acl.txt; sudo -u nobody cat acl.txt

steps.after: `nobody` is neither owner nor in the group, yet it can read. The `+` in `ls -l` warns you that an ACL exists. The group column of `ls -l` now shows the ACL **mask** (`r--`), not the real group rights.

steps.title: File attributes: immutable
steps.text: `chattr +i` marks a file **immutable**. Nobody, not even root, can change, delete or rename it until the flag is removed.

run.output:
rm: cannot remove 'keep.txt': Operation not permitted
rm: cannot remove 'keep.txt': Operation not permitted

run.cmd: sudo chattr -i keep.txt && rm keep.txt && echo removed

quiz.q: A setuid root program is started by you. What is its effective UID?
quiz.explain: The kernel sets the effective UID to the file owner.

quiz.q: What does the setgid bit do on a directory?
options: New files inherit the directory's group
quiz.explain: That is the common use for shared project directories.

quiz.q: How can you see that a file has an ACL in `ls -l`?
Root runs `rm` on an immutable file. What happens?
quiz.explain: The immutable attribute blocks it until `chattr -i`.

check.scenario: During an audit you must list all setuid-root files on a server. Which command do you run, and why are they risky?
check.answer: `find / -xdev -perm -4000 -user root -type f 2>/dev/null`. Each one runs with root rights, so a bug (or a writable/replaceable file) in any of them can give an attacker root. Keep the list short and compare it over time.

interview.a: 755 = rwxr-xr-x (programs, directories), 644 = rw-r--r-- (normal files), 600 = rw------- (private files such as SSH keys). See [the lesson](#/lesson/3/rwx-and-octal).

interview.q: What does x mean on a directory?
interview.a: Permission to enter it and access entries by name. r lists names, w creates/deletes entries (with x).

interview.q: You own a file, you are in its group, the mode is 070. Can you read it?
interview.a: No. The kernel checks the owner class first and stops, so the owner bits (---) apply. See [the lesson](#/lesson/3/owner-group-other).

interview.q: What do setuid, setgid and sticky do?
interview.a: setuid: run as the file's owner. setgid: run as the file's group (on a directory: new files inherit the group). sticky (directories): only an entry's owner can delete it. See [the lesson](#/lesson/3/special-bits-acl-attr).

interview.q: How can root be unable to delete a file?
interview.a: The file has the immutable attribute (`chattr +i`), or the filesystem is read-only, or a mount protects it.
The kernel clears the umask bits from the requested mode of every new file or directory (`mode & ~umask`). Default 022 gives 644 files and 755 directories.

glossary.def: The permission bits of a file: owner, group, other and the special bits.
A per-process mask of permission bits removed from new files and directories.
Mode bit: the program runs with the file owner's effective UID.
Mode bit: run as the file's group; on a directory, new entries inherit its group.
Access Control List: extra per-user and per-group permission entries on a file.
A file flag (chattr +i) that forbids changes, deletion and renaming, even by root.
The user ID the kernel uses for permission checks of a process.
